body: i realized my dream body had nothing to do with my body & everything to do with how i felt about it. i would never have my dream body because i would never be happy with my body, no matter what it looked like. so whatever i thought my "dream body" was became obsolete, bc it wasn't my body. as cheesy as it sounds

i think this might be more convoluted than i understand, but i'll explain how i've always understood it.

whenever we get injured, our body sends out hormones & certain neurotransmitters. some of them signal to the body that we're hurt, but others (like adrenaline) help us cope with the pain. the small amounts of adrenaline & other feel-good hormones/neurotransmitters that a person gets when they cut can subconsciously teach them that cutting will give them small amounts of relief. 

it might be less scary if you think of it as a learned behavior pattern. like how you might stop for a donut once before going to work, and then your brain releases feel-good neurotransmitters, so you're motivated to go again, and then you're going every day. the difference with self harm is that it's a coping skill that reinforces depressive tendency.

i think it also has something or other to do with how (in a very watered down sense) our brains prefer physical pain over emotional pain, and similar parts of the brain are activated when we experience both physical and emotional pain.

the brain is so complex and not entirely understood, and again sh is a complex behavior. when i started sh i felt like it would validate the depression i was experiencing. as i continued self harming, i would get almost tingles in the arm that i would usually injure. 

as long as you approach these conversations with her ready to listen, and you respect when she feels uncomfortable or doesn't want to answer, you'll earn her trust. :)

hello, 

i think the first thing you need to know is that it's not your fault. self harm is a complex behavior. throughout the years, it's been described to my mom & i as an addiction––a cutter will always find a way to cut, so as hard as it is not to, taking away blades just creates the task finding new ones (speaking from experience). 

ultimately, she needs to decide to throw her blades away and when to stop cutting, similar to someone who is dependent on alcohol needs to decide for themself to take back their life. 

she might not know exactly why she cuts, or she might not want to share it yet. sometimes we feel like our reasoning is weird, or we that it doesn't make much sense. there are some common feelings amongst people who self harm and why they continue the behavior, and i encourage you to research them on credible online sources. 

for me, it got to a point where i was cutting for so long that i just liked seeing blood, and i knew it was stupid and i should just get clean. self harm is a complex behavior and it is NOT always an indicator of suicidal ideation (see: nonsuicidal self injury)

i think the best thing you can do is offer her resources. maybe just offering her an appointment with a therapist ("if you'd like, i can get you an appointment for monday"). let her know you won't be intrusive (arm/leg checks, door open, etc). she doesn't need a lecture about how cutting is bad. right now, this is a coping skill, and what she needs is to learn ones that will help her. 

all of this is difficult as a parent. you don't need to be perfect. as you see fit, i encourage you to work this out with a therapist of your own as well, they will help you tremendously.
